I spent most of my time in maternity and pediatrics, working long overnight shifts, assisting with deliveries, monitoring fragile newborns, and improvising when machines broke or medicine ran out. Those early years taught me to think fast and stay calm while everyone around me was frightened. After three years I joined a small community clinic that quietly served women who avoided larger hospitals out of fear of judgment or exposure. My role there stretched far beyond clinical tasks. I triaged patients, drew blood, dressed wounds, administered injections and medications, and sat with people who arrived ashamed, anxious, or in pain. I counselled them, explained their options plainly, and made sure they left feeling treated like human beings. I also managed our patient records, tracked our limited inventory, and placed supply orders whenever our coordinator was away. Beyond that, I trained two junior nurses, teaching them clinical procedures and the harder art of speaking gently to people in distress. Confidentiality mattered enormously, because many of our patients risked real danger simply by coming to us. Through all of it I learned that nursing is part medicine and part trust, and I worked every day to be worthy of both. I would do this work again anywhere. Canada is cold in ways I did not expect. Not just the air that stings my face on the walk to the community centre, but the silence of my own apartment. It is the first space I have ever had entirely to myself, and some nights I do not know what to do with all that stillness. I keep the television on just to hear voices. Back home in Uganda, being seen meant danger. Every gesture, every friendship, every laugh too loud in the wrong place could unravel everything. I learned to make myself small, to speak carefully, to watch other people's eyes before I opened my mouth. That habit does not leave just because the country does. Here, I am invisible in a different way. One face among many on the subway, a name on a list at a newcomer clinic. No one is watching me. No one is reporting me. And somehow that, too, takes getting used to. Safety, I am discovering, has its own texture. It does not feel the way I imagined. I went to a community event last week. There were others like me, from different countries, different stories, same fear slowly thawing. A woman from Kenya touched my hand when I told her where I was from. I cried in the bathroom afterward, quietly, the way I always cry. I am not happy yet. But I think happiness might be something I am now allowed to want. That alone feels like a beginning.
Software developer: For nine years I worked as a software developer in Kyiv, and it was the career I had dreamed of since I was a teenager taking apart computers. I started as a junior engineer straight out of university, writing small features and absorbing everything I could from patient older colleagues who corrected my mistakes without humiliating me. Over the years I grew into a senior engineer and eventually a team lead. The largest and most important part of my career was at a logistics company, where I built and maintained the web applications that tracked thousands of shipments crossing the country every single day. I wrote backend code, designed and optimized our databases, and integrated the many systems that had to communicate reliably for the entire business to function. When something failed at three in the morning, I was usually the one who answered the call and fixed it before any customer noticed a problem. In my final years there I managed a team of four engineers. I planned our projects, reviewed everyone's code, set our technical direction, and mentored the newer staff, always remembering how it felt to be the youngest and least certain person in the room. I worked fluently in several programming languages and never stopped studying new tools and methods. Building dependable systems that real companies relied on gave me deep satisfaction. I take pride in writing clean, careful code, and in leaving every project stronger than I found it. My hands feel useless here. At home they always had something to do. Now I sit in a waiting room with a number, and someone explains things to me slowly, like I am a child. I smile and nod. I understand more English than people expect, but I let them finish. It seems to make them feel better, and right now I have very little else to offer anyone. I am grateful. That is what I tell myself when the frustration rises, when I fill out the same form for the third time, when someone repeats a word louder as though volume is the problem. I came from Kharkiv. The city I grew up in no longer looks like the city I grew up in. My mother is still there. She refuses to leave. Every time we speak, I want to beg her. Every time, I talk about the weather instead. Toronto is enormous. I did not expect the noise, or the way strangers smile at you on the street for no reason. In Ukraine, we do not smile at strangers. It means something is wrong. Here it seems to mean nothing at all, and everything at once. A man at the shelter told me it takes a year before Canada starts to feel real. I do not have the patience for a year. But then I remember what I left behind, and I find the patience. I find it every morning, in a cold apartment, with instant coffee, watching the snow.
Tailor: After my family fled Syria and settled in Lebanon, I worked as a seamstress for four years, and it was where I grew up. I was only sixteen when I started, in a small and crowded tailoring shop tucked into a busy Beirut street. In the beginning the owner trusted me with only the simplest tasks: hemming trousers, sewing on buttons, taking in loose seams. I watched the older women constantly, studying how they held the fabric and guided the needle, and I practiced at home with leftover scraps late into the night until my stitches were straight and even. Within a year I had earned the right to sew whole garments by myself. I made dresses, school uniforms, and curtains, and once a wedding gown that took me two careful weeks to complete. I learned to read and cut patterns, to match fabrics and thread, and to handle delicate materials like silk, chiffon, and lace without tearing or staining them. I worked long days bent over the machine, usually six days a week, often staying late when orders piled up before a holiday. Over time I built my own group of loyal customers who asked for me by name and trusted me with the clothes that mattered most to their families. The pay was small and the hours were hard on my back and eyes, but I became genuinely skilled at my craft. I was proud of every single piece that left my hands finished and clean. I spent four years in Lebanon trying to be invisible. Now a woman at the settlement office looked me in the eye and asked what I need. Just like that. What do you need, Reem? I could not answer. Nobody had asked me that in a very long time. I laughed, and then I apologized for laughing, and she said please don't apologize, and I almost cried right there in the plastic chair. I am twenty-one. I should be figuring out who I am in the normal way, through small embarrassments and bad decisions and friendships that go wrong and then come back. Instead I am doing it in a language still stiff in my mouth, in a city that hums quietly under ice. Montreal is beautiful. That surprised me. I did not let myself imagine beauty before I arrived. Hope felt too dangerous. Even now, allowing good feelings in feels risky, like I might jinx something, like the ground might shift again the way it always has. I video-call my cousins in Beirut and they want to know everything. I describe the snow. I describe the Metro. I describe the bagel I ate that was nothing like what I expected. I leave out how often I sit on the floor of my room and just breathe, counting slowly, the way the counsellor showed me. My French is getting better. I made a joke in French last week and the librarian laughed. It was a small thing. I thought about it for the rest of the day.
Primary school teacher: For more than twenty years I worked as a primary school teacher in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and it was my life's work in the truest sense of those words. I taught children between the ages of six and eleven, mostly reading, writing, and arithmetic, often in crowded classrooms holding more than fifty pupils with far too few books, chalk, or supplies to share among them. I prepared every lesson by hand, marked the children's exercises late into the evening by lamplight, and met regularly with the parents who entrusted their sons and daughters to my care. With so many students and so little material to work with, I learned to hold their attention and keep order without ever raising my voice, relying instead on songs, stories, repetition, and a great deal of patience. I came to know each child by name, and I noticed quickly when one arrived hungry, frightened, or quietly struggling with the lessons. In my final years I took on additional responsibilities beyond the classroom, helping to manage the daily running of the school, organizing the timetable, and mentoring the younger teachers, several of whom I had once taught as small children myself. I watched generation after generation of pupils learn to read their first sentences and write their own names with pride. That achievement, more than any other thing I have done in my life, remains my deepest and most lasting pride as a teacher. I have buried things before. I know how to keep moving. What I did not know is how quiet grief can be in a new place, where no one recognizes your name, where the spices in the grocery store are wrong, where you must begin again at forty-eight. My children are with my sister in Kinshasa. The plan was always to bring them here once I was settled. The plan has not changed. But the distance is a weight I carry in my chest, and some mornings it presses harder than others. I do not let them see it when we call. I keep my voice steady. I tell them about the snow, and they laugh, and that is enough for the moment. Ottawa is orderly. Clean. People wait their turn, hold doors, say sorry when there is nothing to be sorry for. I watch and I study and I remember everything. I have always been a person who watches before she speaks. I was told Canada is cold and people are cold too. That has not been my experience, though I understand why people say it. Warmth here is quieter than I expected. More careful. It arrives in small gestures — a neighbour leaving groceries outside my door, a volunteer sitting with me through a confusing form without checking her phone. I have a notebook where I write things down. French words, English words, bus routes, names of people who have been kind. The notebook is already half full. I am forty-eight years old and I am starting over. The strange thing is, I am not afraid.
Automechanic: In Afghanistan I worked as a car mechanic, and I learned the entire trade with my own two hands, with no school and no manual to guide me. I started very young, helping in my uncle's small and busy garage when I was only fourteen years old. In the beginning my jobs were the simplest ones: sweeping the oily floor, organizing the scattered tools, and passing my uncle whatever he reached for without looking. But I watched everything he did with complete attention, and I asked so many questions that he used to laugh and tell me to stop talking and simply hand him the wrench. Even so, I learned quickly. Within two years I was working full time and taking on real repairs by myself. I fixed cars and motorcycles, replaced engines, clutches, and worn brake pads, changed oil and tires, and brought old, exhausted vehicles back to life when they should have been scrapped years earlier. I learned to diagnose a problem simply by listening carefully to how an engine ran, and to hunt down affordable used parts when new ones were far beyond what our customers could pay. I was young, but people slowly began to ask for me by name and to trust the work I did on the cars their families depended on. By the time I left Afghanistan, I could handle almost any repair in that garage entirely on my own, from the first diagnosis to the final test drive. Everyone keeps asking how I feel. The counsellors, the volunteers, the woman in English class with the big earrings who writes slowly on the whiteboard so we can all keep up. I say I feel okay, because okay is true enough and also because my English for feelings is still very small. The truth longer than okay is that I do not yet know this version of myself. I am waiting to meet him, this person I will become here. I came alone from Kabul. I am the first in my family to be here, which means I carry all of them with me, in every decision, in every application, in every form I fill out with a borrowed pen. I am nineteen and I feel ancient. I also feel like a child. Both things live in me at the same time and I have stopped trying to choose between them. Vancouver is green even in winter. The mountains appeared the first morning out of the clouds and I stopped walking and just stood there on the sidewalk. A man passing asked if I was alright. I said yes. I think I was. I have made one friend. His name is Rayan and he is from Somalia and his English is much better than mine. He taught me how to use the bus app. He showed me where to buy good bread cheaply. Small things matter enormously here, in ways I did not expect and cannot fully explain. My mother calls every Sunday. I tell her I am okay. She tells me she knows.
